values.value: • Move from solution acceptance to buying commitment. • Confirm commercials assumptions, onboarding expectation, stakeholders, and decision timeline. • Ask what is still needed before internal sign-off. • Use the acceptance to ask for a clear next step with date and owner. • Do not let an accepted solution sit without a closure plan.
6|Accepted
Buyer may say, 'Looks good, we will come back.' Response: 'Great. To help move this smoothly, what still needs to happen internally before you can say yes?'
Great sign. Move quickly to commercial close, internal sponsorship, and written next steps.
Low risk. Push toward closure.
Ask: 'Since the solution is accepted, what is the fastest path from here to commercial approval?'
Accepted

• Find out what exactly is under discussion: fit, cost, timing, internal alignment, or risk. • Bring the unresolved points into the open one by one. • Offer a concise summary of the agreed solution and open issues. • Use proof points to reduce uncertainty where needed. • Work towards a defined decision conversation, not open-ended follow-ups.
6|Under discussion
Buyer may say, 'We are reviewing internally.' Response: 'Helpful to know. Which part is still being discussed so I can address that directly rather than follow up blindly?'
Find the exact open points and close them one by one. General follow-ups will only slow this down.
Risk: Discussion without issue list leads to drift.
Ask: 'Which 2 or 3 concerns are still open before you can say yes to the solution?'
Under discussion

• Do not chase with generic reminders alone. • Reconnect around the business problem and ask if priorities have changed. • Give the buyer an easy response path such as a yes/no check on the proposed direction. • If needed, shorten the ask to one focused next step instead of a full deal conversation. • Revive the deal by making re-engagement easy and relevant.
6|No response
Buyer may say nothing at all. Response: 'I wanted to check whether priorities have shifted or whether there is a specific point holding the discussion back.'
Do not keep nudging blindly. Reopen with a sharper message tied to the buyer problem and a specific decision ask.
Risk: Silent deals usually fade.
Say: 'I want to avoid sending noise. Is the silence because of priority, fit, budget, or internal alignment?'
No response

• Treat the rework request as useful buying data, not rejection. • Understand which part needs change: scope, pricing, format, rollout, outcomes, or governance. • Agree what acceptable rework looks like before you redo anything. • Avoid large proposal changes without buyer input or decision-maker visibility. • Resubmit only after confirming the revised version addresses the real concern.
6|Rework necessary
Buyer may say, 'Please revise and resend.' Response: 'Certainly. To make sure the revision lands well, can I confirm the two or three changes that matter most from your side?'
Treat this as a redesign, not a follow-up. Understand what failed and rebuild only around the must-win outcomes.
High risk: Current solution is not landing.
Ask: 'What must change in the solution for it to become acceptable internally?'
Rework necessary
Has the customer principally accepted our proposed solution?
